arxiv:2611.25075.title: Evaluation of machine-learning and deep-learning SPEI drought forecasts against persistence across timescales and lead times in Bangladesh
arxiv:2611.25075.summary: Bangladesh, home to nearly 178 million people, is highly vulnerable to recurring droughts that threaten food security and rural livelihoods. Machine-learning and deep-learning models are increasingly used to forecast drought indices such as the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Most studies report accuracy without a persistence reference, although accumulated indices are strongly autocorrelated, and seldom test drought detection, longer leads or variation between training runs. This study forecast SPEI at 3-, 6- and 12-month timescales one to three months ahead for the eight divisions of Bangladesh, using ERA5 reanalysis checked against 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations. Five models, XGBoost, CNN, Bi-LSTM, CNN-BiLSTM and CEEMDAN-BiLSTM, were trained with five seeds each, scored on accuracy, skill against persistence and drought detection, and interpreted with Shapley values. At a one-month lead, the CNN-BiLSTM and Bi-LSTM beat persistence clearly at SPEI-3 and SPEI-6 (skill 0.408 and 0.350), while at SPEI-12 a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.872 barely exceeded persistence (0.850). Skill and detection could disagree: at SPEI-3 and a three-month lead, XGBoost had the highest skill (0.439) yet detected none of the 119 drought months. Only at SPEI-6 did the forecasts beat persistence significantly and match its detection at all three leads, with fewer false alarms. At SPEI-12, gains were small or absent and varied between seeds. The forecasts kept 76-80% of their correlation against station-derived SPEI and relied mainly on precipitation and lagged SPEI. Forecasts should therefore be judged on skill against persistence and detection across several seeds, not on accuracy alone. In Bangladesh, SPEI-6 forecasts can support early warning up to three months ahead and SPEI-3 forecasts one month ahead, while SPEI-12 is better suited to monitoring.

arxiv:2611.24020.title: Enabling joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation with an atmospheric foundation model
arxiv:2611.24020.summary: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is the main oxidant in the troposphere and accounts for 88% of the methane sink, yet its abundance and trends remain poorly constrained. Satellites observe many of the chemical and meteorological drivers of OH, but assimilating both requires a model that represents chemistry and meteorology together. Existing chemistry-climate models are too expensive for joint data assimilation. Here, we present AuroraChem, a fine-tuned version of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model that jointly simulates meteorology and the GEOS-Chem chemical fields needed to constrain OH. A one-year AuroraChem rollout takes 12 minutes on one GPU. Free rollouts remain stable for one year but do not fully capture seasonal cycles. Using idealized data assimilation, we find that chemical observations can constrain the meteorological state and meteorological observations can constrain the chemical state. Inserting only the chemical fields raises the annual mean spatial correlation of 500 hPa temperature from 0.89 to 0.92 and recovers the moisture and circulation pattern of the Indian summer monsoon. Inserting only the meteorological fields raises the 500 hPa OH correlation from 0.89 to 0.93, close to the 0.94 from inserting the chemical fields themselves, and recovers the OH seasonal cycle. Inserting only NO2 columns sampled at TROPOMI pixels gives an OH correlation of 0.93. These relationships likely reflect learned covariances rather than physical coupling, and covariances are what data assimilation uses to let an observation of one variable update the others. AuroraChem therefore provides a new pathway to joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation.
arxiv:2611.24020.authors: Eliot J. Kim, Eric J. Mei, Peter D. Ivatt, Lee T. Murray, Alexander J. Turner

arxiv:2611.23863.title: Comparing Data-Driven and Numerical Weather Prediction Forecasts of Extreme Weather: A Review
arxiv:2611.23863.summary: Data-driven weather forecasting models, chiefly trained on reanalysis data, now match or beat physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models on most headline scores, but whether this advantage extends to extreme weather is contested. We review peer-reviewed studies that directly compare data-driven forecasts with NWP for extremes, from nowcasting to subseasonal lead times. We discuss grey literature in the outlook but do not include it in the formal review. There is good agreement on the fact that data-driven models mostly outperform NWP on temperature extremes, tropical cyclone tracks and the location of synoptic features across time scales. The evidence is mixed for extreme precipitation and feature-based extreme event detection such as extremes related to atmospheric rivers, while it leans toward better NWP performance for estimating event intensity. For record-breaking events that lie outside the training distribution, the evidence is narrower. Nonetheless, both a systematic global evaluation and several case studies find that physics-based models retain the advantage, with data-driven models underestimating both the frequency and the magnitude of records. Hybrid systems that post-process NWP with machine-learning (ML), or couple data-driven forecasts with physics-based models, deliver some of the largest and most consistent gains. We argue that headline scores, verification choices and case selection explain much of the apparent disagreement in the literature, and provide recommendations for a more trustworthy and interpretable evaluation of data-driven models for extreme and record-breaking weather.
arxiv:2611.23863.authors: Gabriele Messori, Hiu-Wang Lau, Chenyu Dong, Gianmarco Mengaldo, Leonardo Olivetti

arxiv:2611.22641.title: A regime dependent parameterization of the refractive-index structure parameter $C_n^2$
arxiv:2611.22641.summary: Vertical profiles of the refractive-index (RI) structure parameter, $C_n^2$, are required in atmospheric-optics calculations. The Hufnagel--Valley (HV) model is a useful reference profile and it is widely used however, it is difficult to say that it produces consistent results at the observed altitude, magnitude, and thickness of all turbulent layers and it can diverge from realistic measurements in particular height ranges, sites, and stability regimes. This study develops a regime-dependent RI structure parameter considering meteorological conditions and, more importantly, it provides a structure that can be calibrated against measured $C_n^2$ throughout the surface layer (SL), atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), and free atmosphere. The formulation combines SL including distinct unstable, near-neutral, and stable limits; convective ABL; and free-atmospheric turbulence when kinetic-energy and temperature-variance dissipation rates are available. The $C_n^2$ is formed by weighting the contribution of different layers. We use representative, physically plausible meteorological profiles to examine the model's limiting behavior, transitions between atmospheric regimes, continuity, sensitivity to its parameters, and propagation-related differences from the HV 5/7 model. The intended outcome is a measurement-calibrated model that remains physically interpretable across meteorological regimes.
arxiv:2611.22641.authors: Yalçın Ata, Muhsin Caner Gökçe, Yahya Baykal

arxiv:2611.22601.title: Improving Eddy Detection from Wide-Swath Altimetry with Multimodal Data-Driven Models
arxiv:2611.22601.summary: Physically-based eddy detection algorithms usually rely on hard-coded thresholds and constraints that make the detected structures sensitive to small variations in the underlying fields. One way to relax such conditions is the use of machine-learning methodologies that transform the full problem into an optimization process. We present a multimodal, multi-task, data-driven eddy detection framework based on a shallow convolutional U-Net, trained to jointly segment eddy structures and reconstruct the co-located spatial sea surface temperature (SST) anomaly using a dynamically-based reconstruction as target. Two model variants are developed: NADIRnet, trained on conventional nadir altimetry, and SWOTnet, trained through a curriculum that incorporates SWOT-enriched maps. Both models achieve high pixel- and structure-wise detection scores against the ground-truth, with most residual disagreement attributable to boundary placement rather than missed or spurious detections. The coupled SST regression task, enforced through boundary-coupling and gradient-matching loss terms, is shown to sharpen and regularise the detected eddy boundaries. Compared to the dynamically-based reference, both models recover a substantially larger and finer eddy population; notably, SWOTnet's higher-resolution training signal transfers to conventional nadir altimetry thanks to the higher-resolution SST channel, detecting more eddies than a nadir-trained model on the same data. The framework further generalises, even without retraining, to altimetry products and processing levels unseen during training, including SWOT L3 wide-swath retrievals and an independent gridded product. Together with its low computational cost, this framework is thus promising for near-real-time operational deployment and further downstream applications.
arxiv:2611.22601.authors: Matteo Broccoli, Andrea Cipollone, Antonio Bonaduce, Elisa Carli, Florian Le Guillou

arxiv:2611.22496.title: DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence
arxiv:2611.22496.summary: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry. On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.
arxiv:2611.22496.authors: Coen van den Elsen, Laurens Geffert

arxiv:2611.21769.title: Learning Calibrated and Samplable Predictive Distributions of Surface-Ocean $Δp$CO$_2$ Using Tabular Diffusion Models
arxiv:2611.21769.summary: The ocean absorbs almost 30% of anthropogenic CO$_2$ emissions, but quantifying this sink requires estimating surface-ocean CO$_2$ from observations that are sparse in space and time. Most existing machine-learning estimates of this field are deterministic, giving a single value per grid point, with uncertainty approximated post hoc via residuals, ensembles, or prescribed distributions. We instead learn a conditional predictive distribution for each observation: using Treeffuser, a conditional diffusion model with gradient-boosted-tree score functions, we estimate the full predictive distribution of $Δp$CO$_2$ (the sea-air $p$CO$_2$ difference) from 13 environmental, spatial, and temporal predictors. On a held-out SOCAT test set, Treeffuser attains the lowest continuous ranked probability score among the uncertainty-quantification methods evaluated (8.229 $μ$atm) and the coverage closest to the nominal 68% / 95% levels (0.686 / 0.930), while retaining point-prediction skill comparable to a deterministic XGBoost baseline (RMSE 18.4 vs. 17.7 $μ$atm; $R^2$ 0.77 vs. 0.79). These results show that conditional diffusion can provide well-calibrated, observation-level uncertainties while largely preserving point-prediction skill. Because Treeffuser is generative, its samples can support probabilistic analyses of $Δp$CO$_2$; extending this to spatially coherent field reconstruction will require modeling dependence across grid cells and evaluation on spatially held-out data.
arxiv:2611.21769.authors: Gabriele Accarino, Mohammad M. Amirian, Thea H. Heimdal, Amanda R. Fay, Galen A. McKinley, Viviana Acquaviva

arxiv:2611.20251.title: Improving Tropical Cyclone Forecasts through Objective Ensemble Track-Error Reduction
arxiv:2611.20251.summary: Accurate tropical cyclone (TC) track guidance is essential for warnings, evacuation planning, and risk communication, but outlying members and distinct track scenarios can degrade raw ensemble forecasts. Statistical and machine-learning (ML) methods proposed to improve ensemble guidance are difficult to compare because previous studies often use different forecast systems, basins, periods, and verification methods. Using a common verification framework, this study compares six objective methods (four statistical trimming and two ML methods) with the full ensemble mean for 138 TCs forecast by GEFS, MOGREPS-G, and IFS during 2016-2024. Dynamic trimming (DT) is the most consistent statistical method, reducing mean total track error by 8.0%, 13.4%, and 16.1% at short, medium, and long ranges. Its largest benefits occur in high-spread cases, where it can reach 70% of the low-error bound. Short-lead-error trimming (SLET) provides useful delayed guidance after early observations become available, but its improvement decreases with lead time. Regression-mixture clustering (RC) shows potential in low-spread cases and provides the largest improvement over the control run. The gradient boosted tree (GBT) produces the largest medium-range improvement and exceeds the theoretical trimming bound, suggesting strong potential, particularly when the observed track is poorly represented by the ensemble family. However, its 12.8% short-range degradation and gains concentrated in a small subset of cases indicate overcorrection when the ensemble mean is already accurate, highlighting the need for additional constraints. These results provide a consistent basis for using objective error-reduction methods to strengthen TC track guidance for operational decision-making.
arxiv:2611.20251.authors: Shuochen Wang, Mark S. Allen, Auroop R. Ganguly

arxiv:2611.20114.title: A plug-in energy-balance freezing module for transformer frost nowcasting without leaf-sensor inputs
arxiv:2611.20114.summary: Frost protection requires local warnings where leaf-sensor inputs are unavailable. In the frost literature we surveyed, physics entered machine-learning models through inputs, numerical-model coupling, or losses, rather than model structure. We develop a transformer-compatible module that embeds leaf energy-balance physics in freezing-probability forecasts: an energy-balance temperature reference and a learned residual predict leaf temperature, which drives a multiplicative gate imposing a temperature-dependent probability cap. We mathematically prove conditional monotonicity and an alarm boundary, and test whether placing the same information in the output pathway or in attention yields different benefits. We evaluated 12 hourly leads at 19 Korean stations over five frost seasons, with and without leaf-sensor inputs. In the 2025-2026 hold-out season without these inputs, our time-token transformer (PET-E) achieved a lead-mean critical success index (CSI) of 0.516 versus 0.478 for fixed-configuration, joint-lead LightGBM, with significant gains at all 12 leads, and the fraction of alarms at observed leaf temperatures of at least 2 degrees C fell from 0.087 to 0.051 relative to the unmodified backbone. Across the hold-out and a retrospective 2024-2025 evaluation, the module reduced Brier scores and warm-surface alarm fractions in both the time-token transformer and iTransformer, with no significant CSI decrease at any lead. At held-out stations without static or leaf-sensor inputs, both module-equipped backbones exceeded LightGBM at all 12 leads (CSI 0.468 and 0.467 versus 0.437). In the time-token backbone, the temperature pathway reduced this alarm fraction in all four settings, whereas the attention prior increased CSI in three. These findings link an explicit temperature-dependent probability cap to improved forecasts and distinguish output-side from attention-based embedding.
arxiv:2611.20114.authors: Juyeon Kim, Chaeyeon Yi, Yun Am Seo

arxiv:2611.19966.title: Towards GPROF V08: A Machine-Learning Framework for Simulating Passive Microwave Observations of Precipitation
arxiv:2611.19966.summary: Spatially resolved precipitation retrievals based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can improve precipitation estimates from passive microwave (PMW) observations and will be used to implement the next operational PMW retrieval algorithm for the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission. However, the conventional radiative transfer simulations used to extend the retrieval algorithm to the various sensors of the GPM constellation do not provide the spatial coverage required to train CNN-based retrievals. To address this, we introduce a machine-learning-based simulation framework that enables the training of the CNN-based GPROF-NN 3D retrieval algorithm for the full GPM constellation. At the core of this framework is Satformer, a new neural-network architecture that can translate PMW observations between any pair of GPM sensors. The resulting synthetic observations exhibit lower errors than conventional radiative transfer simulations and lead to more accurate precipitation retrievals when used to train GPROF-NN precipitation retrievals. We further demonstrate the applicability of the framework to new instruments by developing GPROF-NN retrievals for the Microwave Imager aboard the Weather System Follow-on Microwave satellite. While GPROF-NN retrievals based on the new simulation framework achieve lower instantaneous retrieval errors and higher correlations compared to independent reference data than conventional retrievals, residual simulation errors can introduce systematic biases in the resulting retrievals. The proposed simulation framework provides a key component for extending GPROF-NN to the full GPM constellation as part of the upcoming operational GPROF V08 retrieval algorithm. The results demonstrate the potential of machine-learning-based simulations to support spatially resolved precipitation retrievals across heterogeneous satellite constellations.
arxiv:2611.19966.authors: Simon Pfreundschuh, Christian D. Kummerow, Paula J. Brown

arxiv:2611.18393.title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
arxiv:2611.18393.summary: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.
arxiv:2611.18393.authors: Kate Duffy, Elise Penn, Tristan Ballard, August Posch, Thomas J. Vandal

arxiv:2611.15266.title: DaYu-TC: a global-regional nested AI system for tropical cyclone forecasting
arxiv:2611.15266.summary: Accurate tropical cyclone intensity forecasts are essential for disaster preparedness, yet persistent intensity underestimation limits the value of artificial intelligence (AI) weather models for predicting these destructive storms. Here we present DaYu-TC, a global-regional nested system that links the preservation of strong-wind and low-pressure signals with high-resolution regional prediction. Its global and regional models share an architecture and extreme-aware training objectives. The regional model combines evolving local states with global forecasts valid at each target time, connecting large-scale environmental information with finer-scale cyclone evolution. In an independent evaluation of 16 western North Pacific tropical cyclones in 2023, the global model retains competitive conventional forecast skill while reducing five-day maximum-wind root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 6-22% relative to other evaluated global AI models. Relative to the global model, regional nesting reduces maximum-wind RMSE by 22.0-33.1% and minimum-pressure RMSE by 28.6-39.8% across 12-120 h. The complete system outperforms concurrent operational high-resolution forecasts from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts for minimum pressure at 12-120 h and maximum wind speed at 48-96 h, with respective RMSE reductions of 26% and 12% at 72 h. Without retraining, the same regional model enhances three other global AI models, reducing overall maximum-wind RMSE by 22.6-28.6%. Five-day forecasts take under one minute on a single GPU. These results establish a transferable multiscale approach to reducing cyclone intensity underestimation, extending advances in AI weather forecasting towards more accurate prediction of high-impact weather events.
arxiv:2611.15266.authors: Runzepu Hou, Feng Zhang, Xin Wu, Xujun Wei, Fenghua Ling, Kan Dai

arxiv:2611.14868.title: Data-driven Reconstruction of the Phase Dynamics for the El Niño-Southern Oscillation Reveals Seasonality and Statistical Synchronization with the Annual Cycle
arxiv:2611.14868.summary: In this study, we treat the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) as a rhythmic system periodically forced by the annual cycle. We examine ENSO event seasonality and synchronization between the annual and ENSO cycles. We compute phase time series for both cycles from sea surface temperature data using a data-driven Koopman operator approach. We then use Bayesian inference to reconstruct phase equations describing how the phases of the two oscillators evolve. The reconstructed two-variable phase equations show that the annual cycle modulates the instantaneous frequency of the fundamental ENSO mode. Stochastic simulations of these equations incorporating the estimated stationary noise indicate that El Niño and La Niña events tend to last longer when they start in boreal summer and that the variability of their durations is greater when they start in boreal spring. Furthermore, the averaged form of the phase equations indicates statistical $3:1$ phase locking between the annual and ENSO cycles, whereas no statistical phase locking is found for the other $m:n$ ratios.

arxiv:2611.14401.title: Discovering Equations for the Thermodynamics of South Asian Monsoon Precipitation
arxiv:2611.14401.summary: South Asian monsoon precipitation depends on the thermodynamic structure of the lower troposphere, but how its ingredients combine to shape precipitation remains unclear, partly because this dependence is nonlocal in the vertical. We use symbolic distillation, which combines neural networks and symbolic regression, to discover interpretable precipitation equations from 21 years of June-August reanalysis data. Neural networks first learn the vertical thermodynamic structure most relevant to precipitation, condensing each variable into a single interpretable feature not tied to a particular vertical grid. Then, symbolic regression derives closed-form equations from these features and the surface state. Our best equation explains 1.5 times as much precipitation variance as a widely used buoyancy-based diagnostic and recovers about 85% of neural network skill while using about a thousand times fewer parameters. Unlike the buoyancy diagnostic, which adds moisture and instability, the equations treat them as competing controls, with the heaviest precipitation occurring when the lower free troposphere is humid. Over ocean, sensible heating is associated with additional precipitation mainly when near-surface air is warm and moist, improving predicted precipitation and its diurnal cycle. Although the learned features were optimized only for precipitation prediction, the equations largely respond to each feature as expected from convective physics, consistent with the reanalysis. These responses reduce the dependence of monsoon precipitation on the entire vertical column to a few simple, testable constraints that could guide data-driven precipitation models to make them more physically consistent.
arxiv:2611.14401.authors: Savannah L. Ferretti, Jane W. Baldwin, Michael S. Pritchard, Tom Beucler

arxiv:2611.13359.title: Reconstructing Boundary Layer Wind Profiles with Machine Learning: A Comparative Study on IGRA Radiosonde Data
arxiv:2611.13359.summary: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) drive short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, yet sparse radiosonde coverage forces practitioners to interpolate them from a handful of physical predictors. We benchmark modern tabular learners against analytical parameterizations on 158,097 IGRA soundings. CatBoost, TabM, and FT-Transformer reduce RMSE to 1.3-1.6 m/s, against approximately 3 m/s for power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits; once the predictor set is fixed the three architectures differ by less than 0.05 m/s, so accuracy is driven by predictors rather than architecture. A cohort analysis of within-bin profile dispersion places an empirical floor of approximately 1.77 m/s on any point-wise predictor that uses standard radiosonde features, consistent with prior eddy-viscosity inversions. A one-dimensional Fourier Neural Operator applied as a post-hoc corrector to frozen tabular predictions reduces near-surface RMSE on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s, while leaving upper-layer error unchanged. Further gains should come from new predictors rather than larger models.
arxiv:2611.13359.authors: Fedor Buzaev, Dmitry Efremenko, Daria Pugacheva, Fedor Ratnikov, Egor Bugaev, Vladimir Gordin

arxiv:2611.12515.title: Is AMOC collapse too unstable in climate models?
arxiv:2611.12515.summary: It has been a long-held paradigm that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation in coupled climate models is too stable, underestimating the possibility of a collapse. A recent analysis of extended simulations to year 2300 in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, CMIP6, demonstrated a partial AMOC collapse where the deep circulation completely vanishes. This collapse was simulated by at least one model in all emission scenarios, and it occurred in every model forced by the highest emission scenario when extended to year 2300. Given the modelling community's previous emphasis on stability in climate models, in this perspective, we explore the alternate possible mechanisms by which the AMOC in CMIP6 might have become too unstable. This is motivated by the lack of evidence of downward trends in the AMOC in the observational records, and a subset of CMIP6 models displaying too high climate sensitivity and too strong sensitivity to aerosol removal, both of which could predispose them toward a spurious collapse. For these reasons, it is critical to evaluate the mechanisms by which CMIP6 models simulate AMOC collapse, to be able to develop programs further investigating the trustworthiness of simulated AMOC collapse scenarios.

arxiv:2611.11918.title: Ensemble Covariance Propagation with Machine Learning Weather Prediction Models in a Realistic Data Assimilation System
arxiv:2611.11918.summary: Integrating machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models into classical data assimilation (DA) workflows requires that they accurately evolve ensemble covariances. We evaluate this capability in a two-way coupled DA system, where an ensemble variational (EnVar) component evolves the mean and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) evolves the covariances. The system is cycled over one month and assimilates a wide range of real-world observations, including microwave radiances. Using the MLWP model GraphCast for the EnKF and the physics-based MPAS model for the EnVar yields ensemble spread and covariances comparable to a reference configuration in which MPAS evolves both components. The resulting EnVar mean achieves consistently lower RMSE against GFS analyses, except near the model top, where spurious correlations degrade performance. These results demonstrate that MLWP models can propagate covariance information in a realistic DA cycling system and provide a proof of concept for their integration into future operational ensemble systems.
arxiv:2611.11918.authors: Simon Toedtli, David Ahijevych, Wei Wang, Chris Snyder

arxiv:2611.12999.title: Direct Multispectral Satellite Nowcasting of Gridded Surface Solar Radiation
arxiv:2611.12999.summary: Surface shortwave radiation (SWR) can change within minutes as clouds evolve, but operational forecasts often trade spatial detail and update frequency for forecast range. Here, we present a numerical-weather-prediction-independent, observation-to-forecast framework that converts sequences of Himawari-9 Level-1 multispectral imagery and solar geometry directly into 24 gridded SWR fields at 10-min intervals for the next 4 h. A controlled six-model experiment in eastern China separates the effects of satellite information from those of temporal self-attention. In the 0-1 h window, the full-multispectral attention model achieves a mean absolute error of 37.9 W/m2 and a root mean square error of 63.7 W/m2, reductions of 21.0% and 19.5% relative to a historical-SWR baseline. Improvements extend across nine subregions and include weaker spatial bias and better structural consistency. Temporal attention does not improve forecasts from historical SWR alone, but becomes effective when supplied with multispectral cloud and thermodynamic signals. Direct multispectral observations therefore provide the precursor information required for high-frequency, spatially resolved SWR nowcasting.
arxiv:2611.12999.authors: Tianyu Xie, Zhaoliang Zeng, Zhehao Liang, Ke Gui, Xutao Zhang, Yaqiang Wang

arxiv:2611.11066.title: Rescene-ESM: an Earth system model built around a frozen AI weather model
arxiv:2611.11066.summary: Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

arxiv:2611.10882.title: Guiding future global temperature distributions with simulations and observations
arxiv:2611.10882.summary: Assessing climate risks requires projections of daily temperature distributions, including rare and spatially widespread extremes. Climate simulations are costly and biased, while correcting them toward observations risks suppressing inter-model differences. We train a single machine-learning emulator, a conditional diffusion model, on seventeen CMIP6 models and ERA5 reanalysis to generate spatially coherent daily temperature fields conditioned on model identity, date, and CO2-equivalent concentration. At sampling time, diffusion guidance reduces model biases by steering each emulated climate-model distribution toward observations, with its strength selected through perfect-model experiments using withheld simulated futures. Observational influence decreases with projection horizon and forcing. Across seventeen synthetic targets, guidance more than halves median biases in the 1st and 99th percentiles of daily temperature, improves probabilistic scores and reliability, and reduces median annual global-mean temperature RMSE by 32-57% across three emission scenarios. In a detailed benchmark, guidance also outperforms established bias corrections on daily-field probabilistic scores. Efficient sampling generates large ensembles without further climate simulations. For example, our framework corrects CMIP6's roughly threefold historical overestimate of extreme-heat coverage, yet projects that concurrent extremes will affect nearly half of global land on a typical day in the 2080s under SSP3-7.0.
arxiv:2611.10882.authors: Francesco Immorlano, Elijah Tavares, Felix Draxler, Juan Nathaniel, Violette Launeau, Duncan Watson-Parris

arxiv:2611.09663.title: RainFlow: Flow Matching for Infrared-Only Quantitative Precipitation Estimation
arxiv:2611.09663.summary: Geostationary infrared imagers observe precipitating systems every 10 to 15 minutes over large areas, but they sense cloud tops rather than the rain beneath. Their brightness temperatures constrain surface rain only weakly, so retrievals trained by regression return a smooth estimate that misses heavy rain and carries no measure of uncertainty. We treat infrared-only retrieval as conditional generation and introduce RainFlow, a flow-matching model that generates ensembles of rain fields from MSG/SEVIRI infrared observations, in a direct and a residual variant. Evaluated against radar over metropolitan France for a full year, the generated members are realistic rain fields, with the observed dry areas, heavy rain and spatial structure, and the ensemble mean is as accurate as a deterministic baseline. Used as probabilities, the ensembles locate heavy rain at scales where the baseline has no skill, and their spread captures most of the retrieval error, with only slight underdispersion. Trained with a time-sampling density that favours the noise end of the generative trajectory, the two variants reach similar skill. The direct variant depends strongly on this choice of density, whereas the residual variant is nearly insensitive to it. Evaluating the generated rain as a function of brightness temperature shows that the ensembles reproduce how rain depends on it over most of the range. It also isolates the remaining gap, an underestimate of both the amount and the variability of rain under the coldest cloud tops, which scores computed over all pixels do not reveal.
arxiv:2611.09663.authors: Matthieu Meignin, Cécile Mallet, Nicolas Viltard

arxiv:2611.09573.title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
arxiv:2611.09573.summary: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.

arxiv:2611.08148.title: Detecting Weather Fronts from Satellite Observations: What Does Reanalysis Add?
arxiv:2611.08148.summary: Weather fronts are transition regions between air masses with contrasting thermodynamic properties and are associated with mid-latitude precipitation and severe weather. We investigate machine learning (ML) methods for detecting weather fronts and quantify the contribution of reanalysis data to performance. We compare two configurations of the same ML model for pixel-wise frontal classification over the North Atlantic and Europe: (1) using only geostationary infrared satellite observations, and (2) additionally using 28 ERA5 reanalysis fields. The satellite-only model achieves a neighbourhood critical success index at a 150 km tolerance (CSI@150) of $0.402$, which lies within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services. The satellite$+$ERA5 model achieves $0.575$, an improvement of $0.173$. Our analysis shows that low-level winds are the least predictable from the satellite representation ($R^2 = 0.23$, compared with $0.88$ for temperature), while removing winds or moisture causes the largest decreases in detection performance.
arxiv:2611.08148.authors: Ioannis Dravilas, Miruna Stoicescu, Roope Tervo, Carlos Horn, Oriol Hinojo Comellas, Sina Montazeri

arxiv:2611.07969.title: Estimating Vertical Ocean Velocity from Horizontal Currents: Linear and Depth-Conditional Neural-Network Approaches on a High-Resolution Regional Ocean Model
arxiv:2611.07969.summary: The vertical component of the ocean velocity, w, is several orders of magnitude smaller than the horizontal components u and v, yet it controls vertical tracer transport, upwelling, and mixed-layer ventilation. Because w is extremely difficult to measure directly and is normally obtained only diagnostically from the continuity equation, predicting it from the horizontal velocity field is a problem of both practical and physical interest. We address this problem with two data-driven methods, a physically-motivated linear baseline and a convolutional neural network conditioned on depth through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM). Both methods are applied to a high-resolution regional simulation of the Coastal and Regional Ocean Community model over the Western Mediterranean, using a sub-region of the south-west Mediterranean Sea as a training region and two independent, out-of-sample regions for validation: the Alboran Sea, with a distinct dynamical regime driven by Atlantic inflow through the Strait of Gibraltar, and a transition region between Almería and Cartagena, between the Alboran Sea and the open western Mediterranean. Once the FiLM network is regularized enough to avoid overfitting to a single training domain, we find that its comparison with the physically interpretable linear baseline is domain- and depth-dependent rather than uniform: near the reference depth, essentially all of the achievable out-of-sample performance on both validation domains is already captured by the linear model, but at the deepest levels tested the FiLM network outperforms the linear baseline on the transition domain, whereas on Alboran it does not.
arxiv:2611.07969.authors: Francesco M. Ventrella, Cristóbal López, Emilio Hernandez-Garcia

arxiv:2611.07094.title: A Deep-Learning Framework for the Generalized Emulation of Atmospheric Radiative Transfer at Microwave Frequencies
arxiv:2611.07094.summary: This paper presents an application of machine learning to the problem of the computational expense of atmospheric radiative transfer calculations from physics-based models. While in recent studies individual emulators have been created that emulate certain radiative transfer schemes for different sensors, we show that a general framework can be applied to emulate the radiative transfer method itself. A fully connected deep neural network has been trained to predict top-of-atmosphere microwave radiances in all-sky conditions over various land, ocean and sea ice surfaces at all frequencies from 1 to 300 GHz, and for all incidence angles from 0 to 65 degrees. The reference models against which the emulator has been trained include an Eddington two-stream radiative transfer model for one-dimensional and pseudo-three-dimensional microwave brightness temperature simulations. This neural network architecture has also been separately trained to reproduce the explicit calculations of the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) for a single microwave imager. In all cases, the model architecture is successfully able predict microwave brightness temperatures by being trained directly on the optical properties of the atmosphere and surface and therefore directly emulating the radiative transfer method. Compared to the explicit schemes used to produce the training data, the GPU-enabled emulator is able to produce brightness temperature simulations more than three orders of magnitude faster and with a root-mean-squared-error less than 0.0348 K, 0.0531 K, and 0.0246 K against the independent test data for the two Eddington models and CRTM, respectively. Additionally, preliminary training using a full 3D Monte Carlo scheme for high-resolution simulations shows promising results for the application of this method to "exact" radiative transfer methods, and these results are discussed in Section IV.
arxiv:2611.07094.authors: Spencer R. Jones, Simon Pfreundschuh, Christian D. Kummerow

arxiv:2611.06539.title: Evaluating the prediction of subgrid eddy kinetic energy from a machine learning model
arxiv:2611.06539.summary: Global climate model resolution is still too coarse to fully resolve mesoscale processes, therefore subgrid closures are required to approximate the feedback of eddies onto the resolved flow. With high-resolution datasets now readily available, there has been a rapid growth in the use of machine learning to develop new eddy closures that could help reduce model biases and uncertainty. In this work we employ an offline learning approach with a convolutional neural network to predict subgrid eddy kinetic energy ($KE_e$), laying the initial groundwork for a machine-learned scale-aware GEOMETRIC eddy closure for the UK's Earth System Model. We address the question of whether global parameterizations are needed or if regional closures are sufficient by evaluating a number of neural network models through region and feature ablation experiments. ML parameterization models generalize to unseen regions when their training data share similar feature and target distributions with those regions. Models that fail to generalize incur distributional shift, or employ different filtering scales for the true eddy kinetic energy field. When holding out features, there is improvement among the generalizable ML models, with some feature spaces leading to improvements in some regions but degrading performance in others. Generally, power spectral density of $KE_e$ tend to diverge at small scales, though some feature spaces are able to minimize this divergence. Overall, the best performing model trained on all regions achieves time-mean and anomaly R2 scores of R2$\approx 0.95$ and R2$\approx 0.8 - 0.9$, respectively.
arxiv:2611.06539.authors: Thomas Wilder, Ranjini Swaminathan, David Storkey, Till Kuhlbrodt

arxiv:2611.05592.title: Distinguishing Initial-Condition and Model Error Using Machine-Learning Weather Models
arxiv:2611.05592.summary: Differentiable weather models allow atmospheric initial conditions to be directly optimized to shadow a known trajectory, which we take from a reanalysis dataset. Here, we extend this optimization to include the forecast model, GraphCast, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare model optimization with initial-condition (IC) optimization, and then joint optimization, where both are tuned simultaneously. When compared against a control forecast initialized with reanalysis data, LoRA and IC optimization individually produce similar improvements. We find similar results when IC and LoRA are jointly optimized across a spectrum of solutions where a tuning coefficient smoothly shifts the weight of the joint optimization from all-LoRA to all-IC; forecast improvement is not unique to the relative contributions of model and IC corrections. To better discriminate the source of error, we introduce a second model, Pangu-Weather, as a supervisor that gates IC updates during joint optimization. This gated optimization is the same as before, except that IC updates at each epoch are accepted only when they improve the forecasts of both models; otherwise, only the LoRA update is accepted. Results show that this cross-model constraint substantially improves agreement between the two models in their response to the same optimized ICs, narrowing the gap in mean forecast error reduction from 64% to 10%. Moreover, when used together, the LoRA and IC corrections from the gated optimization yield GraphCast forecast improvements similar to those from the ungated optimization. These results imply that model error that is encoded in the ungated ICs is shifted to the LoRA corrections via gating, yielding IC corrections that may provide better analysis estimates.
arxiv:2611.05592.authors: P. Trent Vonich, Gregory J. Hakim

arxiv:2611.04892.title: A Multidimensional Evaluation Framework for Artificial Intelligence-Based Ocean State Forecasts
arxiv:2611.04892.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) based ocean state forecasts now approach or surpass those produced by operational ocean forecasting systems as measured by conventional pointwise metrics. However, these metrics may favor spatially smoothed forecasts and cannot determine whether forecast variables remain physically coherent. Forecast evaluation should therefore move beyond overall pointwise accuracy toward assessing forecast trustworthiness. We propose a multidimensional framework comprising overall pointwise accuracy, physical consistency, and distributional consistency. Overall pointwise accuracy summarizes forecast and reference agreement over all valid samples; physical consistency evaluates dynamical balances using model outputs alone; and distributional consistency evaluates distribution tails and multiscale spatial structures. Three AI models were deployed as representative testbeds in a unified operational environment. This comprehensive assessment shows that lower overall pointwise errors cannot preclude substantial dynamical imbalances and suppressed fine-scale variance. Conversely, higher pointwise errors may arise from spatial displacement of coherent structures rather than a poor representation of their amplitude. The results demonstrate that the evaluation of AI ocean forecasting models should be based on the multi-dimensional assessment of forecast trustworthiness, rather than solely relying on a single metric. The study provides a preliminary framework for AI model intercomparison, which is also informative for targeted model refinement and operational implementation.
arxiv:2611.04892.authors: Ziqing Zu, Ye Yuan, Tiejun Ling, Zhi Chen, Xiang Li, Zhiqiang Li

arxiv:2611.04536.title: Machine learning emulators of dynamic global vegetation models for fast gridded carbon budget predictions
arxiv:2611.04536.summary: The land carbon sink explains most of the variability of the atmospheric CO2 growth rate, but the Global Carbon Budget estimates it with dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) run once a year. Emulators could provide it sooner if they reproduce each model outside its training period. Here we show that convolutional neural network emulators of 19 of these models, driven by ERA5 climate and their own past predictions, reproduce the global land sink of these models and its spread over two years not used in training. Global monthly net biome production (NBP) anomalies were reproduced with a median R^2 of 0.81. The error of the multi-model mean annual NBP was at most 0.23 GtC yr^-1. At the grid-cell level, the median R^2 of monthly anomalies was 0.30, partly because of errors that accumulate in the emulated NBP history.
arxiv:2611.04536.authors: Piyu Ke, Xiaofan Gui, Stephen Sitch, Zhu Liu, Xun Li, Jiang Bian

arxiv:2611.04270.title: From Sea Surface Height to Velocity - A Machine Learning Approach
arxiv:2611.04270.summary: Inferring upper-ocean velocity from altimetric sea surface height (SSH) remains challenging below 50~km, scales now resolved by the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission. Conventional methods rely on geostrophic or cyclogeostrophic balance. Here, we demonstrate that deep learning can predict the full velocity vector from SSH and environmental data and recover derivative-based diagnostics, including spectral energy flux. We trained a U-Net encoder--decoder on hourly fields from the pre-SWOT Cape Basin extraction of the LLC4320 ocean simulation, with 1.5-km grid spacing ($11.8$--$15.8^\circ$E, $41$--$45^\circ$S). Inputs were SSH, sea surface temperature (SST), and wind stress; targets were horizontal velocities at the surface and 50~m, where wind influence is weaker. At 50~m, the best model achieves a speed RMSE of $0.049\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, 29% lower than the geostrophic approximation. Predicted relative vorticity has a correlation of 0.93, compared with 0.75 for the geostrophic approximation. The model also recovers divergence with a correlation of 0.66, whereas geostrophic velocity is nondivergent by definition. Tests of training strategies yield four findings: SSH gradients outperform raw SSH as inputs; wind stress is the most useful covariate for total velocity prediction; SST benefits vary seasonally; and including vorticity and divergence in the loss improves accuracy. These results offer a path for transferring high-fidelity simulation physics to SWOT applications, where kilometer-scale SSH snapshots contain superposed balanced and unbalanced signals.
arxiv:2611.04270.authors: Yaswanth Reddy Yaradoddi, Jinbo Wang, Elyes Serghine

arxiv:2611.03925.title: Tropical Cyclone-Following Dataset for Limited-Area Machine Learning Applications
arxiv:2611.03925.summary: This work presents a lightweight dataset of tropical cyclone (TC)-following meteorological variables to facilitate the development and application of machine learning (ML) methods in TC research. Using outputs from our previous climate downscaling and idealized simulations, the dataset is constructed as multichannel video sequences that track TC centers throughout their lifetimes. To demonstrate the dataset utility, we present an application in which a regional ML model is trained to predict TC intensity with explicit incorporation of lateral boundary conditions. Our results highlight the importance of lateral boundary information for predicting TC intensity with ML models inside a limited-area domain, underscoring the need to properly account for lateral boundaries when developing regional ML models for TC intensity forecast.

arxiv:2611.03543.title: Can LLM Agents Improve Imperfect Earth System Model Parameterizations?
arxiv:2611.03543.summary: Earth system models (ESMs) rely on parameterizations to represent unresolved processes such as convection, cloud microphysics, and turbulence. However, translating advances in physical understanding into stable, validated parameterizations and integrating them into ESMs often takes years. Agentic AI could accelerate this process and enable more systematic exploration of design choices. Using warm-rain collision-coalescence as a test case, we evaluate agents' ability to synthesize scientific literature, reimplement published bulk parameterizations, and propose new functional forms as differentiable JAX code. We compare conventional parameterizations, data-driven emulators, and agent-generated closures against high-fidelity superdroplet simulations, repeating unattended experiments across ten language models. With expert guidance or iterative feedback, agents produced executable, differentiable, mass-conserving code, although unattended performance depended strongly on the scheme and language model. Iterative feedback lowered median rollout error for eight of ten models. Retuned physical schemes matched or outperformed many learned parameterizations at substantially lower computational cost, but two of 100 unattended agent-generated closures achieved slightly lower rain-mass error than the most accurate retuned scheme on held-out simulations.

arxiv:2611.02460.title: New Wine in an Old Bottle -- NeuralPOM: A Hybrid Ocean Forecast Model with Differentiable Dynamics and Staged Learning
arxiv:2611.02460.summary: Coarse-grid ocean circulation models rely on empirical subgrid parameterizations that struggle to capture mesoscale eddies, whereas purely data-driven neural forecasters accumulate trajectory drift, violate tracer conservation, and damp small-scale variability over extended integrations. Here we present NeuralPOM, a hybrid ocean forecast model that couples differentiable explicit mode-split and semi-implicit free-surface implementations of the Princeton Ocean Model (POM) to a conservation-constrained neural corrector. The three-dimensional primitive-equation solver advances the ocean state, while the neural network periodically updates the physical fields at high-frequency (1 h) or low-frequency (1 day) intervals under volume, heat, and salt conservation constraints. Using a fine-grid reference dataset exceeding 100,000 model days in a wind-driven double-gyre basin, we introduce a three-stage training procedure comprising offline single-step pretraining, multi-step differentiable training through the ocean solver, and multi-day closed-loop rollout training. Over 100-day forecasts, NeuralPOM reduces errors across all prognostic fields relative to coarse-grid physical closures and direct neural forecasters, preserving mesoscale kinetic energy while improving eddy phase alignment. Controlled ablations show that closed-loop training suppresses multi-day drift, whereas backpropagating gradients through the differentiable solver stabilizes high-frequency coupling. Finally, because high-frequency tracer updates can introduce density anomalies via the equation of state that excite spurious baroclinic pressure gradients, we introduce Density-Normal Damping (DND) to attenuate the density-modifying (diapycnal) tracer component while retaining the density-compensated (isopycnal) correction.
arxiv:2611.02460.authors: Ruiqi Shu, Guangliang Liu, Ruijian Gou, Tianrun Gao, Haomin Wen, Hao Li

arxiv:2611.01614.title: Sonny-ENS: demystifying machine-learning ensemble weather forecasting
arxiv:2611.01614.summary: Every weather forecast is uncertain, and decisions from flood warnings to energy trading depend on how well that uncertainty is quantified. Machine-learning (ML) ensembles now quantify it better than the best physics-based ensemble, yet two things about them remain opaque: whether their skill requires hundreds to thousands of accelerator-days of training, and how a network with a simple source of randomness produces a spread that follows the flow. Here we introduce Sonny-ENS, an ensemble of three 68.9-million-parameter networks with Monte Carlo dropout, trained on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) in 2.7 A40 GPU-days. On 2022, it has a lower CRPS than the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble (ENS) on 96% of 570 targets and an 8.3% lower mean CRPS at lead times of 1-10 days. It outperforms the operational GenCast on 69% of the targets, and a 51-member, 15-day forecast takes 69 s on one GPU. Ablations identify the ingredients of this skill, and a Kolmogorov-Arnold sparse autoencoder shows that dropout injects uncertainty mainly in the tropics, whereas the spread grows where the atmosphere is baroclinically unstable (spatial correlation 0.91 with the Eady growth rate). Skillful probabilistic weather forecasts are therefore within reach of a single GPU server.

arxiv:2610.42130.title: Value of Adding AI Weather Model Ensembles to a Multi-model Probabilistic Blend
arxiv:2610.42130.summary: Many weather forecasting organizations use a multi-model blend of ensemble members from different prediction systems to obtain a more accurate forecast. Recent studies have shown that blending deterministic AI-based models alongside physics-based models improves the overall forecast skill. However, the incorporation of an ensemble AI-based model into a multi-model blend is yet to be investigated. This study explores the value of blending the ensemble version of the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS-CRPS) with the Met Office's convection permitting physics-based ensemble, MOGREPS-UK. We show that blending site temperature (and wind speed) forecasts over the United Kingdom from both ensemble physics-based and ensemble AI-based models leads to an increase in overall forecast skill spatially, across lead times and across exceedance thresholds, especially when the models have different error characteristics. By decomposing the continuous ranked probability score of the blend into component means and diversity terms, we show that a more accurate blend can be achieved by assigning more weight to more skillful models and using models with complementary errors. For example, we show that a blend of MOGREPS-UK with either AIFS-CRPS or the physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) is better than a blend of IFS and AIFS-CRPS which are not very diverse. This has implications for the importance of weather model diversity and may lend weight to different model development approaches being pursued in tandem. We also demonstrate that calibrating AIFS-CRPS forecasts yields an increase in forecast skill comparable to calibrated ensemble physics-based forecasts, and calibrating the source forecasts before blending and the blended forecast after blending improves the overall forecast accuracy.
arxiv:2610.42130.authors: Harris Sop Nkuiate, Gavin Evans, Christopher A. T. Ferro, Frank Kwasniok, Caroline Bain, Stefan Siegert

arxiv:2610.42111.title: SATFRONT: Detecting Atmospheric Fronts with Satellite Data using Machine Learning
arxiv:2610.42111.summary: Atmospheric fronts are associated with much of the high-impact weather in the mid-latitudes, yet their identification and classification remain largely manual and subjective. Existing deep learning approaches rely primarily on gridded reanalysis or forecast data, limiting their applicability to satellite observations available for time-critical applications. We introduce SATFRONT, a machine learning framework for detecting cold, warm, and occluded fronts over Europe from geostationary satellite observations, with reanalysis data as an optional additional input. The model is trained on frontal analyses from five European national meteorological services and evaluated against UK Met Office analyses for 2024. Using satellite observations alone, SATFRONT achieves a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.428 at a 150 km tolerance, within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services (0.277-0.501) and higher than that of an operational rule-based front detector that uses satellite data (0.133). Adding ERA5 reanalysis increases the CSI to 0.591. ERA5 substantially improves the placement of individual fronts, although its effect on their annual spatial distribution varies by front type. These results demonstrate that cold, warm, and occluded fronts can be detected directly from geostationary satellite observations, providing a basis for automated frontal analyses at the high temporal frequency required for time-critical applications.
arxiv:2610.42111.authors: Ioannis Dravilas, Miruna Stoicescu, Roope Tervo, Carlos Horn, Oriol Hinojo Comellas, Sina Montazeri

arxiv:2610.41052.title: Machine Learning Sensor Fusion for Water Vapor Radiometry based Tropospheric Delay Calibration
arxiv:2610.41052.summary: The next-generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) intends to use 22 GHz water vapor radiometry (WVR) to correct for tropospheric phase fluctuations in its high-frequency bands. However, current delay-retrieval methods do not reach the required accuracy and reliability. As a remedy, we propose a machine-learning based retrieval concept and a preliminary architecture, framed as heterogeneous, multi-rate sensor fusion. Atmospheric reanalysis profiles and surface weather set the context in which per-antenna WVR spectra are used to estimate excess path by a Kalman filter whose parameters are learned from high-cadence calibrator phases. The method is being developed, with planned first validation on the 183 GHz WVR system of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).
arxiv:2610.41052.authors: T. K. Sridharan, Yoshiharu Asaki, Brian E. Svoboda

arxiv:2610.40304.title: Causal-prior-constrained deep learning for rapid-intensification warning of western North Pacific tropical cyclones
arxiv:2610.40304.summary: Rapid intensification (RI) is one of the most dangerous and unpredictable phases of tropical cyclones, and its environmental and structural drivers are difficult to identify and separate in observations. Here we introduce CausalVisionRI, a causal-prior-constrained deep-learning system for 24-h RI warning in the western North Pacific. It integrates infrared remote sensing imagery, atmospheric and oceanic fields, and an observationally discovered causal graph into a unified model. The graph and eight sign-verified effects on 24-h intensity change provide an auditable causal prior for training. Discovered from 522 cyclones in 2000-2017, it identifies causal pathways linking atmospheric and oceanic conditions, the cyclone's dynamical and structural state, and its 24-h intensity change. On a forward holdout covering 2020-2024 and 3,004 records, the five-member ensemble achieves a Brier skill score (BSS) of 0.259 relative to a fixed development climatology, significantly exceeding four reference systems; the three LDA baselines reach at most 0.105. It also attains higher detection rates than a published knowledge-block scheme and a reconstructed contrastive-learning scheme at matched false-detection rates under our USA 30-kt standard and the published RITCF standard. Ablations show that the graph pathway adds 0.032 BSS across the holdout and 0.063 over 2020-2021, indicating that the gain concentrates in the time period adjacent to the estimation window. A deep-learning model constrained by observationally discovered causal structure thus offers a new route to physically informed RI warning.
arxiv:2610.40304.authors: Xinrui Li, Yijun Jin, Yifan Dong, Shoujuan Shu

arxiv:2610.39334.title: SD3: The First Operationally-Proven, Fully Heterogeneous-Accelerated Global Kilometer-Scale Model with Inline Physics Architecture
arxiv:2610.39334.summary: We present Super Dynamics on the Cube (SD3), the first operationally-proven, fully heterogeneous-accelerated global kilometer-scale model. Through a full-stack reconstruction in native CUDA C, SD3 introduces an "Inline Physics" architecture that deeply couples its non-hydrostatic cubed-sphere dynamical core with fast physical processes. This design maintains high physical consistency, ensures energy and mass conservation, and mitigates "Grey Zone" mismatches. Five years of continuous operational forecasting, together with validation against diverse observations, demonstrates the scientific fidelity of SD3. Recently, SD3 achieved an unprecedented 205.7 simulated days per day at global 1.5 km resolution using 24576 GPUs. SD3 establishes a hardware-agnostic, portable, and reproducible paradigm across diverse Exascale ecosystems. Beyond weather and climate research, SD3 offers a transformative paradigm for the HPC community and the next-generation Digital Twin Earth to establish a robust, high-performance blueprint for the future of Earth system modeling.
arxiv:2610.39334.authors: Yuan Liang, Xiaomin Hu, Xi Chen, Jingsheng Zhu, Li Yang, Leisheng Li

arxiv:2610.37325.title: Scale-aware and spatially-localised optimisation of kilometre-scale MLWP models
arxiv:2610.37325.summary: Preserving fine-scale structure without degrading spatial accuracy is a central challenge for kilometre-scale machine-learning weather prediction (MLWP). We introduce a loss based on the dual-tree complex wavelet transform that constrains atmospheric fields jointly by scale, location, and orientation. We evaluate its performance using an experimental joint global--regional FastNet configuration, which produces \SI{1.5}{km} forecasts over the UK alongside $\sim$\SI{31}{km} global forecasts. Relative to both mean-squared error (MSE) and an FFT-based spectral objective, the wavelet loss substantially improves spectral fidelity. Compared with MSE training, it maintains similar pointwise performance, improves neighbourhood-based verification, and produces sharper precipitation fields with more realistic intensity distributions. These results demonstrate that spatially localised wavelet constraints can preserve multiscale atmospheric structure while largely avoiding the loss of pointwise accuracy associated with globally supported spectral objectives.
arxiv:2610.37325.authors: James Chappell, Sophie Luise Arana, Jack Bowyer, Matthew Burnand, Alejandro Coca-Castro, Evangeline Corcoran

arxiv:2610.36944.title: Impact of Cumulus Parameterization and Cloud Microphysics on WRF Simulation of an Extreme Rainfall Event over Maharashtra, India: A 3 by 3 Factorial Assessment
arxiv:2610.36944.summary: Simulating extreme monsoon rainfall over the Konkan coast and Western Ghats remains challenging at 9 km resolution, where convection is partly resolved and partly parameterised. This study evaluates the sensitivity of Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations of the 5-7 July 2026 Maharashtra rainfall event to cumulus and cloud microphysics schemes. Nine simulations employed a 3 x 3 factorial design combining WSM6, WDM6 and Thompson microphysics with Kain-Fritsch, Tiedtke and Grell-Freitas cumulus schemes. Rainfall was evaluated against IMD 0.25-degree gridded observations, with IMERG and ERA5 as additional references. A descriptive factorial decomposition showed that cumulus parameterisation accounted for 97.3% of across-experiment variation in mean rainfall, 88.2% in RMSE and 84.7% in spatial correlation, while microphysics contributed 2.0%, 2.1% and 9.3%, respectively. Kain-Fritsch produced the highest spatial correlations (0.533-0.581) but substantially overestimated rainfall. Tiedtke achieved the smallest mean biases and RMSE, although compensating regional errors concealed a 28-34% rainfall deficit over the Konkan-Ghats belt and substantial underestimation on 7 July. Grell-Freitas showed large wet biases and relatively high RMSE. All nine simulations displaced the event-total rainfall maximum approximately 140-195 km northward. WSM6-Tiedtke achieved the lowest RMSE, whereas Thompson-Kain-Fritsch better represented the rainfall spatial pattern. The findings demonstrate that, for this event and fixed model configuration, cumulus parameterisation exerted substantially greater influence on simulated rainfall than cloud microphysics. However, a single-event, single-member experimental design does not establish a universally optimal physics configuration.

arxiv:2610.36301.title: Spatially-Adaptive Neural-Network Based Extraction of Significant Wave Heights from HF Radar Data
arxiv:2610.36301.summary: Significant wave height (SWH) retrieval from high-frequency (HF) radar data conventionally relies on Doppler-spectrum processing and interpretation of the weak second-order scattering continuum. This article investigates adaptive spatial processing for time-domain SWH estimation using ordered envelope statistics. In our previous study, a physics-guided linear ordered-statistics estimator (LOSE), motivated by first-order rough-surface scattering assumptions and radar-envelope statistics, mapped the largest rank-ordered magnitudes of Bartlett-beamformed voltages to buoy-observed SWH through least-squares regression. The LOSE framework is extended using three trainable complex spatial filters initialized around the buoy look direction. Ordered magnitudes are extracted independently from each spatial output, concatenated, and mapped to SWH through least-squares regression, while the spatial weights are optimized using gradient-based updates. Both estimators use causal sliding-window averaging. Evaluation used measurements from a 13.385-MHz, 12-receiver element WERA radar at Argentia, Canada, paired with directional-wave buoy observations. Under a common chronological training-evaluation partition, the selected adaptive configuration reduced root-mean-square error by approximately $14.3\%$, while maintaining the Pearson correlation coefficient at $0.949$. These results support the potential of adaptive multi-beam processing to improve time-domain SWH estimation relative to fixed Bartlett-based LOSE. Feature counts and smoothing windows were selected using the evaluation interval; independent testing is therefore needed to establish the generality of the improvement.

arxiv:2610.36297.title: FASST: A Compact Stateless Atmosphere Model for Long-Term Ocean Coupling
arxiv:2610.36297.summary: Coupled climate simulations are computationally expensive, largely because of the atmosphere. We introduce FASST, a coupled climate model that retains the prognostic POP2 ocean while replacing the atmosphere and sea ice with lightweight U-Net emulators. The atmospheric emulator is diagnostic, predicting surface fluxes from the evolving ocean-ice state every $6$ simulated hours, while the sea-ice emulator advances the ice state monthly. For $140$ years of unforced integration, FASST maintains a stable global-mean climate without SST restoring, with post-transient global-mean SST of $291.30 \pm 0.22\mathrm{K}$ compared with $291.25 \pm 0.10\mathrm{K}$ in CESM$2$ piControl. FASST also captures interannual Niño-$3.4$ variability, although with weaker amplitude than CESM ($0.62\mathrm{K}$ versus $1.02\mathrm{K}$). These results demonstrate that a stateless learned atmosphere can sustain stable, free-running coupled climate simulations over century-scale integrations.
arxiv:2610.36297.authors: Pratham Aggarwal, Duncan Watson-Parris, William E. Chapman

arxiv:2610.36186.title: Towards operational data-driven regional weather forecasting: extreme-event skill and near-real-time verification with HRRRCast
arxiv:2610.36186.summary: Improving convective-scale skill in data-driven regional weather models requires better representing rare high-impact events, training at native resolution, broadening variable output, and demonstrating performance in real-time settings. Here, we evaluate these challenges using HRRRCast, a data-driven convection-allowing emulator trained on the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) analysis data. HRRRCast combines native 3-km training, moderate sigmoid-weighted loss reweighting for reflectivity and precipitation, and broader system improvements including expansion of the training archive from 3 to 9 years (2016--2025), increased vertical resolution, expanded outputs, and architectural upgrades. The weighted loss improves high-threshold skill while preserving common-event behavior. Native-resolution training avoids aliasing from 6-km subsampling and substantially improves fractions skill score at convective scales, with gains that persist across pooling windows. HRRRCast has also been running in near-real-time mode for the past year. In seven months of independent observation-based verification, HRRRCast ensemble means improve several near-surface metrics relative to operational HRRR and maintain strong precipitation and reflectivity performance. Single-member reflectivity skill is strongest at 20--30 dBZ; at 40 dBZ, skill is near parity at 6-km pooling and better at pooling radii $\geq$30 km. Precipitation skill remains competitive through 1 in/h and extends to about 3 in/h in the best recent configuration. A focused comparison with HREF further shows useful low-cost probabilistic guidance for 3-h precipitation. At storm scale, HRRRCast exhibits a displacement--structure trade-off, with generally better storm placement than storm morphology.
arxiv:2610.36186.authors: Daniel Abdi, Isidora Jankov, Vanderlei Vargas, Paul Madden, Emily Carpenter, Travis Wilson

arxiv:2610.35693.title: GNN-VIEW: Visual Inspection and Explanation of Graph-based Earth-System Models
arxiv:2610.35693.summary: Machine learning Earth-system models are becoming increasingly important, and so is their development. Graph-based models, one of the most prominent approaches, allow developers to constrain the learning process before training via graph connectivity. Yet, developing these models remains challenging: the graph is built algorithmically with little intuition about the final result beyond static plotting, which requires extra work and is often not detailed enough. Even after successful training, how the model arrives at forecasts remains obscure. We present GNN-VIEW, an interactive browser-based tool that supports the development of such systems. GNN-VIEW exposes the graph's information pathways, allowing model developers to debug the graph structure before training. After training, GNN-VIEW uses attribution-based explainability to reveal which input features are used by the trained model for a given forecast. This helps developers understand why a model fails. We showcase the usefulness of GNN-VIEW in the construction stage of a graph for an ocean forecasting model, and in explaining poorly predicted precipitation of a trained weather forecasting model during Hurricane Laura.
arxiv:2610.35693.authors: Alessandro Lucatelli, Ferdinand Unterhuber, Katharina Krenzer, Mennatallah El-Assady, Benedikt Soja, Christina Humer

arxiv:2610.33609.title: Satellite-derived bathymetry of Arabian Gulf ports under leakage-free validation: a multi-site benchmark of empirical, machine-learning and deep-learning models against 285,000 multibeam soundings, with an outlook for UAE waters
arxiv:2610.33609.summary: Satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) is often proposed as a low-cost complement to multibeam surveys of ports, but its accuracy is seldom measured on an area the model has never seen. We test SDB in the turbid, shallow and tidal waters of the Abu Dhabi coast against 285,619 multibeam soundings from twelve surveys at six port areas, reduced to Lowest Astronomical Tide. The Stumpf ratio, the Lyzenga transform, a monotonic gradient-boosted tree model (LightGBM) and a U-Net ensemble were trained on 72 Sentinel-2 images and tested in transfer to an unseen site and with local control (about 20% of a site's soundings, spatial blocks beyond a 225 m buffer). The validation design changed the result more than the model: the same LightGBM model gave 0.57 m RMSE under a random pixel split, 1.30 m under spatial blocks and 1.66 m at an unseen site. In transfer the Stumpf ratio (1.45 m) was not beaten by LightGBM, the U-Net or Lyzenga. With local control a hybrid of the tree output and the band ratio reached 1.11 m over 0-11 m, 67% of pixels within the IHO S-44 Order 2 tolerance and a conformal 95% interval with 95% observed coverage; in clear water it reached 0.29-0.53 m. The seabed could not be read beyond 11 m, and summer images were five to six times more turbid than winter ones. ICESat-2 ATL24 agreed with the surveys to 0.25 m after a depth-dependent offset was removed. A 60 m reconnaissance mosaic of 17,200 km2 of the UAE coast, calibrated cell by cell on ICESat-2 without any vessel survey, reached 1.42 m RMSE on held-out blocks over half of the product. Sentinel-2 SDB with about a hundred control depths per image is a usable reconnaissance and change-monitoring tool in these waters to about 10 m; it does not meet S-44 Order 1 without local control, and accuracies from random splits should not be taken as operational accuracy.
arxiv:2610.33609.authors: Muhammad Saeed, Mohamed H. Alhosani, Dmitry Mikhaylov, Yasser F. Al Wahedi

arxiv:2610.32438.title: Data Quality Audit and Bivariate Temperature-Humidity Analysis of a Long-Term LoRaWAN Network: Anomaly Detection, PCA, Clustering and Machine Learning
arxiv:2610.32438.summary: Long-term environmental IoT/LPWAN deployments often aggregate heterogeneous data streams from diverse devices without systematic auditing of each variable's actual coverage prior to analysis-an increased risk when multiple sensor types coexist within the same network.
